extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate mathematics students (people who write mathematical proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing clear, correct, and readable mathematical proofs for coursework and research, emphasizing prose narration, precision, motivation, and appropriate detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Know who is reading and what they already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For homework: write to convince a fellow student in the same class. Adjust level of explanation, background, and detail to the intended reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ordinary prose narrative rather than formal symbolic statements or two-column proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "There is an overwhelming consensus that an ordinary prose narrative is much better suited to this purpose than formal symbolic statements." Paragraph-style proofs are easier to read than symbolic or two-column proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose proofs in complete sentences with correct punctuation and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fragments, run-ons, dangling modifiers; maintain subject-verb agreement, parallel structure, and correct spelling. Proper English increases clarity and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear exposition and intuitive explanations; state proof method up front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't be stingy with intuitive explanations. State at the beginning what type of proof you're using (e.g., "we will prove the contrapositive", "by induction").

rubrics_metrics.name: Include motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why definitions are made as they are and why the theorem might be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how one might have been led to the proof, why the proof is structured this way, and how the result will be used. This explanatory material is essential to good exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person singular sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer "we" instead of "I" except when referring to yourself explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to the inclusive "we" (writer + reader); use "I" only when really referring to the author's personal actions or views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of shorthand and abbreviations in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abbreviations such as s.t., w.r.t., w.l.o.g., iff in running text (they're acceptable on the blackboard). Exceptions: i.e., e.g. (with the comma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the proof after writing to catch errors and improve exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read end-to-end after thinking you're done. Later items recommend proofreading again after a wait or by someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what you're proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Precede the proof with a precise English statement of the theorem being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the goal explicit so the reader knows exactly what will be established before entering the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label your theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use theorem/proposition/lemma/corollary labels to signal importance and role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use *Theorem* for important results, *Proposition* for interesting but less important results, *Lemma* for results primarily used in proofs of other statements, and *Corollary* for easy consequences of prior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly mark the start and end of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the word "Proof" and end with a QED symbol (or equivalent) to signal completion to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every term is defined, every symbol is introduced, and every claim is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each statement ask: What does it mean? (every term well-defined; every symbolic name previously defined or quantified before its first use) and Why is it true? (justify by axiom, previously proved theorem, definition, hypothesis, previous step, or rules of logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include more than just the logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine formulas with explanatory prose describing why steps follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersperse formulas with words about why one step follows from another to minimize the reader's work; avoid leaving the reader to fill in too many logical gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the right amount of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sufficient derivations so the reader experiences understanding without unnecessary tedium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If you think you probably know roughly how an argument would go but it seems too tedious to work through in detail, then you need to work through it!" Aim to produce the reader's "Aha!" experience—include detail that makes the key ideas clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs. informal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Signal when you are giving formal logical steps versus informal motivation or intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal material = definitions and rigorous logical steps; informal material = motivation, intuition, sketches. Make the distinction easy for the reader to track (so they know when to expect rigor versus intuition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread again (fresh eyes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisit the proof after a break or have another person read it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreading after a wait or by someone else helps catch errors and exposes unclear explanations you might have missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-line vs. displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose in-line for single symbols/short formulas and displayed (centered) for large or important formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered formulas must be displayed. Use displayed formulas for clarity and emphasis when expressions are large or central to the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulas must function grammatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Every formula should be incorporated into the sentence grammar; never leave a formula as a sentence fragment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formulas either as a noun (object) or as a clause (with a relation as verb). Read sentences including formulas aloud to check grammatical integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read each sentence aloud (including formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory checking helps detect grammatical and clarity issues involving formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud forces you to supply words and connectors that ensure grammatical and logical flow, catching mistakes invisible on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displayed formula at end of sentence requires punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A displayed formula that ends a sentence should be followed by a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a repeated emphasis: maintain normal sentence punctuation even when the last element is a displayed equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't begin a sentence with a math symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with symbols; reword to begin with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences that start with a symbol can be jarring or ungrammatical; introduce the object in words instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adjacent in-line formulas separated only by punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put two in-line formulas next to each other separated only by punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert a word or phrase between in-line formulas to preserve readability and grammatical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations/operators should connect formulas, not English words
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators like >, =, etc., should relate mathematical expressions; avoid using them to connect English fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of BAD style: "If x is real and >2" — rewrite so the relation clearly attaches to the mathematical term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical-symbol shorthand in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not replace English words with logical symbols (∃, ∀, ⇒, ⇔, ∴, ∵) in running text, with limited exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: ⇒ and ⇔ are acceptable between symbolic statements. Otherwise spell out quantifiers and logical connectives in words for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format built-up expressions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Large sums, integrals, matrices, and fractions should be displayed or written to fit on a line; use slashes for simple in-line fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure built-up expressions do not break line flow; prefer display mode for complex constructs and slashes for compact in-line fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple-equality syntax correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Chains like a = b = c = d imply each equality is true and the chain reads forward; only mix relations that satisfy transitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful mixing relations; the reader interprets chained equalities/transitive relations straightforwardly, so ensure each step is valid under transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Math Writing framework (precision + motivation + prose + detail + proofreading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee's summary: precision, motivation, paragraph prose, appropriate detail, and proofreading are distinct evaluation axes for good math writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five axes as an evaluation checklist: ensure precise definitions and justifications, provide motivation and intuition, prefer paragraph prose, include the right amount of detail to produce understanding, and proofread (possibly with fresh eyes).
